Chapter 10 · 第十章

Bringing It All Together: Navigating Technical Leadership融会贯通：驾驭技术领导力

— PDF p.321 —

Technical leadership is a balancing act. It's a role that demands clarity, empathy, technical depth, and strategic awareness, often all at once. Throughout this chapter, I'll look at how to bring these elements together in practice as interconnected parts of your day-to-day work.

技术领导力是一场平衡术。这个角色要求你同时具备清晰的判断力、同理心、技术深度和战略视野——而且往往是同时具备。在本章中，我将探讨如何在日常工作中把这些要素作为相互关联的部分整合到实践中。

I'll start by exploring one of your most high-leverage responsibilities: growing the people around you. Next, I'll shift focus to stakeholder management. Your ability to represent your team, align across departments, and communicate technical ideas clearly to nontechnical partners is a defining part of the role. I'll walk through how to identify the right stakeholders, manage those relationships intentionally, and adapt your communication to influence effectively.

我首先会探讨你最具杠杆效应的职责之一：培养身边的人。接下来，我会把焦点转向干系人管理。你能否代表团队发声、跨部门对齐、把技术思路清晰地传达给非技术伙伴，是这个角色的核心定义。我会带你梳理如何识别正确的干系人、有意识地经营这些关系，并根据对象调整沟通方式以实现有效影响。

Finally, I'll unpack some of the most common, and often unspoken, challenges in aligning tech with the business. Whether it's getting buy-in for technical decisions, figuring out how your impact is measured, or managing the emotional and mental load of the role, this chapter offers practical strategies for navigating the messy, high-stakes reality of tech leadership.

最后，我会拆解技术与业务对齐过程中一些最常见、也往往是不言自明的挑战。无论是为技术决策争取支持、搞清楚你的影响力如何被衡量，还是管理这个角色带来的情绪与心理负荷，本章都会给出可落地的策略，帮你驾驭技术领导力中混乱而高风险的真实局面。

This is where everything comes together: your technical voice, your people instincts, your strategic thinking, and your ability to sustain it all without burning out.

这是一切融会贯通的地方：你的技术判断力、你对人的直觉、你的战略思维，以及你在不被 burnout（职业倦怠）击垮的前提下持续输出这一切的能力。

Developing and Growing Technical Talent培养与发展技术人才

Growing the people around you is an expectation that usually comes with a senior role. As a tech lead, it's about taking this to the next level.

培养身边的人，通常是高级别岗位的应有之义。而作为技术负责人，你要做的是把这件事提升到新的层次。

— PDF p.322 —

This doesn't necessarily mean doing more pairing or supporting more individuals directly. It's about stepping back and thinking more strategically about your team's growth: leveraging team-wide opportunities for development rather than focusing only on individuals. It also involves greater influence over things like budgets and the types of learning support your team can access.

这并不一定意味着你要做更多结对、或直接辅导更多人。它意味着退一步，从更战略的层面思考团队的成长：利用面向整个团队的发展机会，而不是只盯着个人；同时也意味着你要在预算、团队可获得的学习支持类型等事项上拥有更大的话语权。

With that broader perspective in mind, this section will explore how to identify your team's learning needs, support their technical growth with the right tools and opportunities, and help them strengthen the soft skills that turn capable engineers into trusted collaborators and future leaders.

带着这种更宽广的视角，本节将探讨如何识别团队的学习需求、用合适的工具与机会支持他们的技术成长，并帮助他们强化那些把能干的工程师变成值得信赖的协作者与未来领导者的软技能。

Assess and Identify Learning Needs评估并识别学习需求

As a tech lead, part of your responsibility is to make sure your team has the right mix of technical and soft skills to deliver on what's expected. That starts with being intentional about understanding where your team is today and where they need to grow.

作为技术负责人，你的职责之一是确保团队具备技术与软技能的合理搭配，以交付被期待的成果。这始于有意识地了解团队当前所处的位置，以及他们需要在哪些方面成长。

Start by looking at your context. Are you in the middle of a migration? Building something new? Maintaining legacy systems? Each of these requires different strengths. Your team might be great at launching new projects but struggle with long-term maintenance. Or the other way around.

先看你的处境：你们正在做迁移吗？在做新东西吗？还是在维护遗留系统？每一种情况需要的优势都不同。你的团队可能擅长启动新项目，却不擅长长期维护；也可能正好相反。

I once led a team that got the opportunity to build a brand-new product. It was a high-visibility project, and we were excited to take it on. But the catch was this: it was a prototype. We had to move fast, prove the product's viability, and skip over things like full automation and perfect test coverage.

我曾经带过一支团队，得到了一个打造全新产品的机会。那是一个高关注度的项目，我们都很兴奋。但关键在于：那是一个原型。我们必须快速推进、验证产品可行性，并且要跳过诸如完整自动化、完美测试覆盖率之类的事情。

Our team came from a different world. We were used to working on a revenue-generating monolith with a "do it right" mindset: TDD (test-driven development), deep up-front clarification, robust processes. This new initiative demanded speed, iteration, and scrappy fixes, completely the opposite of what we were used to.

我们的团队来自另一个世界。我们习惯了在一个产生收入的单体系统上工作，秉持着"把事做对"的心态：TDD（测试驱动开发）、前期深度澄清、稳健的流程。而这个新倡议要求的是速度、迭代和灵活打补丁，与我们过去习惯的一切完全相反。

We took on the challenge, but the friction was real. Team members were uncomfortable with the shortcuts. Stakeholders were frustrated by delays. Everyone was out of their comfort zone. After some settling-in time, we started to find our rhythm. But it took deliberate effort, including lots of conversations and iteration. This taught me a valuable lesson: before you take on work that demands a different mindset and skills, assess whether your team is equipped for it, and if not, plan for how you'll support them through that shift.

我们接下了挑战，但摩擦是真实存在的。团队成员对这些"捷径"感到不安，干系人对延迟感到沮丧，每个人都走出了舒适区。经过一段时间的磨合，我们开始找到节奏。但这需要刻意的努力，包括大量沟通和迭代。这件事给我上了宝贵的一课：在接手需要不同心态和技能的工作之前，先评估团队是否具备相应能力；如果不具备，就要规划好如何支持他们完成这种转变。

That's why it's worth doing regular checkpoints with your team, especially before jumping into a new challenge. Here are some questions you can explore together to assess where you are and where you want to grow next:

因此，值得和团队定期做检查点，尤其是在迎接新挑战之前。下面这些问题可以一起探讨，用来评估你们现在所处的位置，以及接下来想往哪里成长：

— PDF p.323 —
  • What parts of our system feel fragile or hard to change?我们系统中哪些部分感觉脆弱或难以改动？
  • Are there areas where we rely heavily on one person's knowledge?有没有哪些领域我们严重依赖某一个人的知识？
  • What's something new we've wanted to try but haven't felt ready for?有什么新东西我们一直想试，但又觉得还没准备好？
  • What patterns do we notice in our recent incidents or blockers?在最近的事故或阻塞中，我们注意到了什么模式？
  • Where do we feel like we're guessing rather than deciding with confidence?在哪些地方我们感觉是在猜，而不是有把握地做决定？
  • What are we curious to learn more about?我们对什么东西好奇，想了解更多？
  • What skills would make our day-to-day work smoother?掌握哪些技能会让我们的日常工作更顺畅？
  • How do we currently share knowledge, and what's missing?我们目前是如何共享知识的？还缺什么？
  • What would help us grow more effectively as a team?什么能帮助我们作为一个团队更有效地成长？

Once you've gathered this input, look for patterns. Are there recurring challenges? Common frustrations?

收集到这些输入之后，去寻找模式。有没有反复出现的挑战？有没有共同的挫败感？

All of these give you clues about where the learning gaps are.

所有这些都在告诉你，学习缺口在哪里。

Don't forget to balance team-wide patterns with individual needs. Every developer is on a different growth path. Some may be ready to step into mentoring roles or lead initiatives. Others may need support just getting comfortable with basic technical tasks. Hold both levels in mind: what the team needs as a whole and what each person needs to thrive.

别忘了在团队层面的共性和个人需求之间取得平衡。每位开发者都走在不同的成长路径上。有些人可能已经准备好承担辅导角色或牵头某些倡议；另一些人可能连熟悉基本技术任务都需要支持。两个层面都要放在心上：团队作为整体需要什么，以及每个人要绽放各自需要什么。

Next, align those learning needs with what's coming. What features are on the roadmap? Is there a big migration planned? Are you moving to the cloud or adopting a new architecture? You want to invest in skills that help the team deliver value, not just what's technically interesting. For example, if the business is focusing on an upcoming cloud migration, it might not make sense to invest time in exploring a new web framework right now.

接下来，把这些学习需求与即将到来的事情对齐。路线图上有哪些功能？有没有大的迁移计划？你们要上云或采用新架构吗？你要投资的是能帮团队交付价值的技能，而不只是技术上有趣的东西。比如，如果业务正在聚焦即将到来的云迁移，那么此时投入时间去研究一个新的 Web 框架可能就不太划算。

Once you've identified the most important learning areas, make a plan. You don't have to fix everything at once. Pick one or two priorities, set a goal, and define how you'll track progress. For example, if you want to build a stronger feedback culture, measure how often feedback conversations are happening. Make it visible, and revisit it often.

一旦识别出最重要的学习领域，就制定计划。你不必一下子解决所有问题。挑出一两个优先项，设定目标，并定义如何追踪进展。比如，如果你想建立更强的反馈文化，就去衡量反馈对话发生的频率。让它可见，并经常复盘。

Continuously upskilling your team is a team effort. Involve your team in assessing needs and shaping priorities. Partner with your product manager or engineering manager to align growth with delivery needs. Use one-on-ones to validate direction, get personal insight, and ensure that growth goals reflect both individual aspirations and the evolving needs of the business.

持续提升团队技能是一项团队工程。让团队参与评估需求、塑造优先级。与产品经理或工程经理合作，让成长与交付需求对齐。利用一对一来验证方向、获取个人洞察，并确保成长目标既反映个人抱负，也反映业务不断变化的需求。

— PDF p.324 —

By consistently assessing and addressing your team's learning needs, you increase the team's ability to deliver and adapt to any context.

通过持续评估并满足团队的学习需求，你就在提升团队在任何情境下交付与适应的能力。

Tools for Upskilling the Whole Team面向整个团队的技能提升工具

Once you've identified the growth areas for your team, it's time to act. There are many ways to upskill your team, but not every method fits every context. Your job as a tech lead is to be intentional about which tools to use, when to use them, and how to integrate them into the team's daily work.

一旦识别出团队的成长领域，就该行动了。提升团队技能的方式很多，但不是每种方法都适合所有情境。作为技术负责人，你的工作是有意识地选择用哪些工具、什么时候用、以及如何把它们融入团队的日常工作。

If your entire team needs to build technical strength in a particular area—say, a new framework, architectural pattern, or development practice—focus on collective learning. Here are a few tools you can use:

如果整个团队都需要在某个特定领域建立技术实力——比如一个新框架、一种架构模式或一项开发实践——那就聚焦集体学习。下面是一些可以使用的工具：

Dedicated learning time专门的学习时间

Talk to your manager or stakeholders to secure protected time for learning. This could be a learning day each sprint or a short-term drop in delivery expectations.

与你的经理或干系人沟通，争取受保护的学习时间。这可以是每个迭代中的一个学习日，也可以是短期内降低交付预期。

One simple strategy is to integrate learning time directly into your estimations. Just like you'd account for code reviews or testing, learning has an impact on delivery. Making it explicit in planning helps set the right expectations and prevents it from being pushed aside when deadlines get tight.

一个简单的策略是把学习时间直接纳入估算。就像你会为代码评审或测试留出时间一样，学习也会影响交付。在计划阶段把它明确写出来，有助于设定正确的预期，避免在截止日期紧张时被挤掉。

Knowledge-sharing sessions知识分享会

Run short talks, lightning rounds, or brown-bag lunches. These are great for spreading expertise across the team. These internal talks are ideal when the budget is tight and your team already has internal experts.

组织简短的分享、闪电演讲或自带午餐的 brown-bag 学习会。这些都非常适合在团队内部传播专业知识。当预算紧张、而团队里已经有内部专家时，这类内部分享是最理想的选择。

I remember this time when my team had to learn Scala. Our tech lead at the time planned a full week of Scala training, bringing in a Scala trainer from another office to help us. It was a great way to get us started.

我记得有一次我们团队要学 Scala。当时的技术负责人安排了整整一周的 Scala 培训，从另一个办公室请来一位 Scala 培训师来带我们。那是一个很好的入门方式。

I also find daily tech huddles to be useful for encouraging others to share important learnings in a more informal way. These short check-ins after standup give people space to mention discoveries, surface blockers, or discuss small implementation decisions that others might benefit from.

我也发现每日的技术小聚（tech huddle）很有用，可以鼓励大家以更非正式的方式分享重要的学习收获。这些站会后的简短碰头，给大家留出空间去提到新发现、抛出阻塞问题，或者讨论一些别人可能从中受益的小型实现决策。

Pair programming or mob programming结对编程或mob编程

These work particularly well when knowledge levels vary across the team.

当团队内知识水平参差不平时，这些方式尤其有效。

— PDF p.325 —

Pair programming is one of the most effective tools for growth. I've seen it again and again in the teams I've worked with. The strongest learning happens when people sit together and work through real problems, live in the code, sharing context and solutions as they go.

结对编程是最有效的成长工具之一。在我合作过的团队里，这一点被反复验证。最深刻的学习发生在人们坐在一起、在真实代码里共同解决真实问题、边做边分享上下文与方案的时候。

Mob programming extends this concept further, where the entire team works together at the same time, on the same task, using a single computer. While it might seem inefficient at first glance, it can be incredibly powerful for surfacing hidden knowledge and building collective ownership of the codebase, especially in areas where no one has much context.

Mob（群体）编程把这个概念推得更远：整个团队同一时间、围绕同一个任务、共用一台电脑工作。乍看之下可能显得低效，但对于把隐性知识暴露出来、建立对代码库的集体归属感，它可能极其强大——尤其是在那些没人有太多上下文的领域。

That said, mob programming tends to work best in very specific situations, like exploring unfamiliar parts of the system or onboarding new team members. It also requires a skilled facilitator to keep everyone engaged and ensure the session stays productive. When done poorly, it can leave people feeling like they're not learning much or that they're not contributing. Like many collaborative practices, its effectiveness comes down to how intentionally it's run.

话虽如此，mob 编程往往只在非常特定的场景下效果最好，比如探索系统中不熟悉的部分、或带新成员入职。它还需要一位有经验的引导者来保持大家的投入、确保讨论富有成效。如果做得不好，会让人觉得没学到什么、也觉得自己没做出贡献。和许多协作实践一样，它的效果取决于你有意识地去组织它。

Hackathons or innovation days黑客松或创新日

Use these to experiment with new tools or build quick prototypes. I've seen lots of great features come out of hackathon ideas; some even made it to production. As a plus, they boost creativity and are a great team-building exercise.

用它们来试验新工具或快速搭建原型。我见过很多优秀功能就来自黑客松上的点子，有些甚至最终上了生产环境。此外，它们还能激发创造力，也是很好的团队建设活动。

To make them successful, keep the structure simple: set aside a focused time window (a day or two), let teams self-organize around ideas, and create a low-pressure, playful atmosphere. Encourage demos at the end as a chance to share and celebrate learning.

想让它们成功，结构要简单：留出一段专注的时间窗口（一两天），让团队围绕点子自行组织，营造一种低压力、好玩的氛围。最后鼓励大家做演示，作为分享和庆祝学习成果的机会。

Post-incident reviews事故后复盘

Postmortems are a great learning opportunity for the team, if you run them right. I dive into how to make the most out of these sessions in the section "Dealing with Incidents" on page 254.

如果你做得对，事后复盘（postmortem）是团队绝佳的学习机会。我在第 254 页"处理事故"一节中详细讲了如何充分利用这些环节。

Pairing with other teams与其他团队结对

If another team already has experience in a tech you're picking up, ask to shadow or pair with them. You can also explore the option of inviting someone from that team to run a couple of sessions for your group or be available to answer questions. In one case, we even brought a developer into our team temporarily to teach us how to use a specific tool, something none of us had experience with, and it really helped.

如果另一个团队已经在你正在学习的技术上有经验，就请求去旁听或与他们结对。你也可以考虑邀请对方团队的人来给你们讲几场、或者随时答疑。有一次，我们甚至临时把一位开发者调到我们团队，教我们使用一款没人有经验的工具，效果真的很好。

— PDF p.326 —

When it comes to soft skills, like communication, collaboration, giving and receiving feedback, or even basic Slack etiquette, these are often assumed rather than explicitly taught.

谈到软技能——比如沟通、协作、给予与接受反馈，甚至基本的 Slack 礼仪——这些东西往往被默认你应该会，而不是被明确教过。

But, just like with tech skills, you can run targeted sessions focused on improving them. I've seen teams benefit from short workshops or informal discussions around things like how to write helpful code reviews, how to have difficult conversations, or how to ask for help effectively. These can be facilitated internally or by bringing in external coaches.

但和技术技能一样，你也可以围绕它们组织有针对性的提升活动。我见过很多团队从短工作坊或非正式讨论中受益，主题包括：如何写出有帮助的代码评审意见、如何进行困难对话、如何有效地求助。这些活动可以由内部主持，也可以请外部教练来带。

They're a great way to introduce useful concepts and trigger reflection, but real growth doesn't happen in a single session. Soft skills take time, repetition, and consistent practice to build.

它们是引入有用概念、触发反思的好方式，但真正的成长不会在一次活动中发生。软技能需要时间、重复和持续练习才能建立起来。

That's where process comes in. Processes shape behavior. If your team's routines don't require interaction, interaction won't happen. I've worked with teams where developers barely spoke to each other—no standups, no retros, no shared planning—so no wonder collaboration fell short.

这就是流程发挥作用的地方。流程塑造行为。如果团队的日常节奏不要求互动，互动就不会发生。我曾合作过一些团队，开发者之间几乎不说话——没有站会、没有复盘、没有共同计划——那么协作不到位也就不足为奇了。

To build soft skills, bake collaboration into your team's day-to-day operations:

要建立软技能，就把协作嵌进团队的日常运营中：

  • Hold daily standups, weekly planning, and regular retros to create moments for alignment and feedback.举行每日站会、每周计划会和定期复盘，制造对齐与反馈的时刻。
  • Encourage shared problem solving through pair programming, whiteboarding sessions, and tech huddles.通过结对编程、白板讨论和技术小聚，鼓励共同解决问题。
  • Rotate service ownership to break down silos and build shared responsibility.轮换服务所有权，打破孤岛，建立共同责任。
  • Run regular team rituals that include space for feedback, self-reflection, and improving how the team works together, not just what they build.组织定期的团队仪式，其中留出空间用于反馈、自我反思，以及改进团队"如何一起工作"——而不仅仅是"在做什么"。
  • Organize hackathons or "Lunch and Learn" sessions.组织黑客松或"午餐学习"（Lunch and Learn）活动。

You'll find more techniques in the section "Enabling Collaboration Inside the Team" on page 209.

你可以在第 209 页"促进团队内部协作"一节中找到更多技巧。

These shared routines help normalize healthy communication habits and give everyone practice in the soft skills they need to grow.

这些共享的日常节奏，会让健康的沟通习惯变得正常化，并让每个人都在实践中练习他们成长所需的软技能。

Upskilling a team is about choosing the right tools for your context and making learning part of how your team works every day. Whether it's technical skills or soft skills, the most impactful growth happens when learning is integrated into your team's routines and shaped by what your team actually needs. Be intentional: pick what fits, adapt as you go, and create an environment where people can build new skills through practice, reflection, and shared experience.

提升团队技能，关键是为你的情境选对工具，并把学习变成团队每天工作方式的一部分。无论是技术技能还是软技能，最有影响力的成长发生在学习被融入团队日常节奏、并由团队真实需求塑造的时候。要有意识：选合适的、边走边调整、创造一个让大家能通过实践、反思和共同经验来建立新技能的环境。

— PDF p.327 —

Tools for Upskilling Individuals面向个人的技能提升工具

Combine your team-wide efforts with individual growth plans.

把面向整个团队的努力，与个人成长计划结合起来。

Use your one-on-ones to explore each person's aspirations and knowledge gaps, help them build a growth plan (you can help them apply the steps from the section "Developing a Personal Growth Plan" on page 38), track how they're progressing, and help them connect their growth with upcoming work.

利用一对一来探索每个人的抱负与知识缺口，帮他们建立成长计划（你可以帮助他们应用第 38 页"制定个人成长计划"一节中的步骤），追踪他们的进展，并帮助他们把成长与即将到来的工作联系起来。

Feedback is one of the most powerful tools we have for growth. It shows us what we're doing well, where we need to improve, and how others experience our work.

反馈是我们成长最有力的工具之一。它告诉我们什么做得好、哪里需要改进，以及别人如何看待我们的工作。

Here is how you can use it to help individuals develop their technical skills:

下面是你如何利用反馈来帮助个人发展技术技能：

Getting feedback on pull requests从 Pull Request 获取反馈

One common example is through PR reviews. Developers can track their improvement by the kind of feedback they receive: Are the comments mostly about syntax and formatting, or are they shifting toward deeper questions about design and performance? Are PRs getting approved faster over time, with fewer revisions? These signals can reveal a lot about a developer's growth and confidence in their work.

一个常见的例子就是通过 PR（Pull Request）评审。开发者可以通过收到的反馈类型来追踪自己的进步：评论主要是关于语法和格式，还是正在转向关于设计和性能的更深入问题？PR 是否随时间变得审批更快、修改次数更少？这些信号能透露一个开发者的成长以及对自己工作信心的很多信息。

Getting feedback on technical solutions从技术方案获取反馈

Another great opportunity for technical feedback is during solution design. If someone wants to improve their architectural thinking, they can take the lead on proposing a solution for a new feature. Many teams use shared documents for this; sometimes called TDs (technical designs), RFCs (requests for comments), or architecture proposals. The idea is to write down the plan and share it with relevant stakeholders: team members, other teams, architects, senior engineers.

另一个获取技术反馈的好时机是在方案设计阶段。如果有人想提升架构思维，可以让他牵头为一个新功能提出方案。很多团队为此使用共享文档；有时叫 TD（technical design，技术设计）、RFC（request for comments，意见征集）或架构提案。核心思路是把计划写下来，分享给相关干系人：团队成员、其他团队、架构师、资深工程师。

The feedback that follows is incredibly valuable. It can reveal edge cases they hadn't considered, surface technical risks, or even validate their thinking. Either way, it's a learning moment, and a clear signal of how their current skills are perceived by others.

随之而来的反馈极其宝贵。它可以揭示他们没考虑到的边界情况、暴露技术风险，甚至验证他们的思路。无论哪种情况，这都是一个学习时刻，也是一个清晰信号——告诉他们当前技能在别人眼中是什么样子。

Once you've supported your team in growing their technical expertise, it's time to focus on the other side of the equation: soft skills. These are the skills that turn strong developers into great collaborators, mentors, and future leaders.

一旦你支持团队在技术专长上有所成长，就该把注意力放到等式的另一边：软技能。正是这些技能，把优秀的开发者变成出色的协作者、导师和未来的领导者。

I've been helping techies develop their soft skills for years. I'm an engineer at heart, so I approach soft-skill development just like any technical growth problem: define what to improve, identify the steps to improve it, test something new,

我多年来一直在帮助技术人发展软技能。我骨子里是个工程师，所以我处理软技能发展的方式和处理任何技术成长问题一样：定义要改进什么、找出改进的步骤、尝试新做法、

— PDF p.328 —

reflect on what worked and what didn't, and adapt your process and behavior to include the things that worked.

反思哪些有效、哪些无效，然后调整你的流程和行为，把有效的做法固化下来。

I've used this process time and again, both as a coach and as a tech lead, to help engineers grow. And it's a process you can apply too, for your own development or to support your team as they build their soft skills.

我作为教练和技术负责人，一次又一次地用这个流程来帮助工程师成长。这也是一个你可以应用的流程——不管是用于你自己的发展，还是用来支持团队构建软技能。

In the upcoming sections, I break it down, step by step.

在接下来的小节里，我会一步步拆解这个流程。

Start开始

You don't need a perfect starting point, just a real one. Look around your team or your current collaboration challenges and pick one thing that's not working as well as you'd like. Maybe you're struggling to give constructive feedback. Maybe you're often misunderstood in meetings.

你不需要一个完美的起点，只需要一个真实的起点。看看你的团队或你当前的协作挑战，挑出一件不如你意的事情。也许你难以给出建设性反馈；也许你在会议上经常被人误解。

Pick one problem. Then define a small win. For example, if you want to become better at giving feedback, make a commitment like "This week, I'll give one piece of constructive feedback to a team member." If your goal is to improve meeting facilitation, try "In the next planning session, I'll have a clear structure and keep people on track."

挑一个问题。然后定义一个小胜利。比如，如果你想更擅长给出反馈，就做一个承诺："这周，我要给一位团队成员一条建设性反馈。"如果你的目标是提升会议主持能力，就试试："下次计划会，我要拿出一个清晰的结构，并让大家不跑题。"

Define what success looks like by defining your "why."

通过定义你的"为什么"，来定义成功长什么样。

You might think the why is obvious, but after coaching hundreds of tech professionals, I can tell you it's not always that straightforward. We all have different motivations. And your motivation, the why behind your goal, will shape how you define success.

你可能觉得"为什么"显而易见，但在教练过几百位技术从业者之后，我可以告诉你，事情并不总是这么简单。我们每个人的动机都不同。而你的动机——你目标背后的那个"为什么"——会塑造你对成功的定义。

Let's take the example "I want to become better at giving feedback." Now ask yourself, why? Is it because your manager told you to? Is it because people don't seem to take your feedback seriously? Is it because you've noticed things you want to bring up but don't know how? Is it because giving feedback is part of your job expectations?

我们拿"我想更擅长给出反馈"这个例子来看看。现在问自己：为什么？是因为你的经理让你这么做吗？是因为别人好像不把你的反馈当回事吗？是因为你注意到有些事想提出来、却不知道怎么开口吗？还是因为给出反馈本来就是你岗位要求的一部分？

Each of these whys points to a different version of success:

每一个"为什么"都指向一个不同版本的成功：

  • If your manager told you, success might mean getting a "meets expectations" rating on feedback in your next review.如果是经理让你做的，成功可能意味着下次绩效评估中，反馈这一项拿到"符合预期"。
  • If people don't take your feedback seriously, success could be having someone act on your input or ask follow-up questions.如果是别人不把你的反馈当回事，成功可能意味着有人真的采纳了你的意见，或者追问了后续问题。
— PDF p.329 —
  • If you want to speak up more, success might be delivering one clear, constructive piece of feedback to a team member next week.如果是你想更多地发声，成功可能意味着下周就向一位团队成员给出一条清晰、有建设性的反馈。
  • If it's part of your role, success could be getting input from your team about how they perceive your feedback skills.如果是岗位职责的一部分，成功可能意味着从团队那里收集到他们对你反馈能力的看法。

As you can see, your why determines what progress looks like, and that clarity will guide your next step: taking action.

如你所见，你的"为什么"决定了进步长什么样；而这份清晰，会指引你的下一步——采取行动。

Apply one change应用一个改变

This is the uncomfortable part. Get out of your comfort zone and try something new to address the problem.

这是让人不舒服的部分。走出你的舒适区，尝试一些新做法来解决这个问题。

If you usually avoid speaking in meetings, maybe your one change is preparing a point ahead of time and saying it early.

如果你通常在会议上不发言，那你的一个改变可能是：提前准备好一个观点，并尽早把它说出来。

If you struggle with giving feedback, you might try using a framework like SBI and drafting your message in advance.

如果你在给出反馈上有困难，可以试试用 SBI 这样的框架，并提前打好草稿。

Not sure what change to make? Here is how you can get some ideas:

不确定要做什么改变？下面这些方式可以帮你获得一些灵感：

Explore resources on the topic of interest探索感兴趣主题的相关资源

Read a book, take a course, or search online for how others have tackled similar challenges. Even a short article or video can give you a helpful idea.

读一本书、上一门课，或者上网搜搜别人是怎么应对类似挑战的。哪怕是一篇短文或一段视频，都能给你一个有用的点子。

Use what's available利用现有资源

If your company offers a development budget, make use of it, for conferences, external training, or coaching.

如果公司提供发展预算，就用起来——用来参加会议、外部培训或请教练。

Talk to someone找人聊聊

Reach out to a trusted mentor or coach. They can help you think through the challenge, spot patterns you may not see, and suggest approaches that fit your style.

找一位你信任的导师或教练。他们可以帮你梳理这个挑战、发现你可能没看到的模式，并建议适合你风格的做法。

Observe others观察他人

Look around. Who's great at the skill you're working on? What do they do differently? Try borrowing one of their habits or approaches and see how it fits your style.

看看周围。谁擅长你正在修炼的这项技能？他们做得有什么不同？试着借用他们的某个习惯或做法，看看是否适合你的风格。

Progress often comes from small, repeated steps.

进步往往来自微小而重复的步骤。

— PDF p.330 —

Reflect反思

What worked? What didn't?

什么有效？什么没效？

This is a key step that often gets skipped in the process of growth. People get caught up in the doing, rushing from one challenge to the next, often repeating the same patterns without realizing it. Reflection makes the growth process intentional. It's how you avoid running in circles, repeating mistakes, and missing out on key insights. It helps you spot what worked and double down on it, amplifying growth far more effectively than focusing only on fixing what went wrong.

这是成长过程中一个关键、却经常被跳过的步骤。人们一头扎在做事里，从一个挑战赶往下一个挑战，常常在不知不觉中重复同样的模式。反思让成长过程变得有意识。它让你避免原地转圈、重复犯错、错过关键洞见。它帮你识别什么有效并加倍投入——比起只盯着修好出问题的部分，这种方式能更有效地放大成长。

To actually understand what worked and what didn't, self-reflection alone isn't enough. You need external input. Soft skills are about human interaction, so the most accurate way to assess them is through feedback: how others experience the change. Any behavior shift will affect the people around you, and their perspective is the most valuable data you can get.

要真正搞清楚什么有效、什么没效，光靠自我反思是不够的。你需要外部输入。软技能关乎人与人的互动，所以评估它们最准确的方式就是通过反馈：别人如何体验你的改变。任何行为改变都会影响身边的人，而他们的视角是你能获得的最有价值的数据。

Ask for feedback consistently, especially after moments where soft skills are in play. For example, if you're working on speaking up more in meetings and you share an idea, follow up with a colleague: "How clear was I in that point I made earlier?" The best time to ask is right after the moment happens, when the experience is still fresh and the insight is sharp.

持续地寻求反馈，尤其是在软技能发挥作用的场合之后。比如，如果你正在修炼在会议上更多发言，并且刚刚分享了一个点子，就跟进问一位同事："我刚才那个观点表达清楚吗？"最佳时机就是事情发生之后立刻问，趁体验还新鲜、洞见还锐利。

Adapt调整

Integrate what worked into your habits. Let go of what didn't.

把有效的做法融入你的习惯，放下无效的做法。

Of course, this is easier said than done. Really incorporating a new behavior takes effort. When we're under stress, we tend to fall back on familiar habits, even if they're not helpful. That's why it requires intentional repetition, preparation ahead of time, and a steady commitment to making the new behavior stick.

当然，说起来容易做起来难。真正把一个新行为内化需要努力。当我们处于压力之下时，往往会退回到熟悉的习惯里——即使那些习惯没什么用。这就是为什么它需要有意识的重复、提前准备，以及让新行为生根发芽的稳定承诺。

Tracking your progress is what keeps the motivation alive. Noticing small wins along the way helps you see that you're moving forward. Mark every step, big or small. Even discovering what doesn't work gives you direction. That insight alone is valuable because it tells you what to avoid and where to focus next. Reflection is about identifying what's working so you can do more of it. In fact, doubling down on what works can have a bigger impact on your growth than focusing only on fixing what's broken. And, as a plus, you're also creating a list of accomplishments and learnings, helpful both when you're feeling stuck and for future reference, like proving growth during performance reviews.

追踪你的进展，是保持动力的关键。一路上注意到小胜利，能帮你看到自己在前进。标记每一步，无论大小。即便是发现什么无效，也给了你方向。仅仅是这个洞见本身就很有价值，因为它告诉你要避免什么、下一步聚焦哪里。反思的意义在于识别什么在起作用，好让你做得更多。事实上，加倍投入有效的部分，对你成长的影响可能比只盯着修补破损处更大。而且还有一个额外好处：你同时也在积累一份成就与学习清单——在你感到卡住时它有用，在未来也有用，比如在绩效评估中证明自己的成长。

It's easy to get caught in the loop of constant improvement without recognizing progress. If you focus only on what you haven't mastered yet, you risk losing

人很容易陷入"持续改进"的循环，却没有意识到自己的进步。如果你只盯着自己还没掌握的东西，就有失去动力的风险。

— PDF p.331 —

motivation. Instead, regularly recognize what is working. That's what helps you stay energized and engaged, instead of burning out or giving up midway through the journey.

相反，要定期认可什么在起作用。这才是帮你保持活力与投入、而不是在半路 burnout 或放弃的关键。

The process of growth is continuous and cyclical. Once the steps—start, apply, reflect, adapt—have been completed, it's time to go through them again. The same situation can be revisited with a new strategy, or a completely different challenge can be tackled.

成长的过程是持续而循环的。一旦走完了"开始—应用—反思—调整"这几步，就该再走一遍。同一个情境可以用新策略重新面对，也可以去挑战一个完全不同的问题。

The great thing about improving a soft skill is that the benefits ripple across everything else you do. You can't isolate one behavior; working on something like listening, for example, inevitably improves how you give feedback, how you build trust, and how you support your team members. As people grow in one area, their overall ability to collaborate, lead, and communicate improves too.

提升一项软技能最棒的一点是，它的收益会涟漪般扩散到你做的其他所有事情上。你无法把某个行为孤立出来；比如修炼倾听，不可避免地会改善你给出反馈的方式、建立信任的方式，以及支持团队成员的方式。当人们在一个领域成长时，他们整体的协作、领导与沟通能力也会随之提升。

And the impact isn't just individual. When more people on your team level up their soft skills, the entire team dynamic shifts. Communication becomes clearer, misunderstandings happen less often, and conflict becomes easier to manage, or avoided entirely. It's not just about being "nicer" or more "professional." Strong soft skills lead to stronger collaboration and better results.

而且影响不止于个人。当团队里更多人提升了软技能，整个团队的动态都会改变。沟通变得更清晰，误解更少发生，冲突更容易管理，甚至被完全避免。这不仅仅是变得"更友善"或更"专业"的问题。强大的软技能会带来更强的协作和更好的结果。

Some strategies are universally useful, whether someone is deepening their technical expertise or working on communication, leadership, or collaboration. These are great tools to have in your tech lead toolbox:

有些策略放之四海而皆准——无论一个人是在深化技术专长，还是在修炼沟通、领导力或协作。这些都是技术负责人工具箱里非常棒的工具：

Encourage people to make use of their development budget, if one is available如果有发展预算，鼓励大家用起来

You'd be surprised how often this budget goes unused. Many engineers avoid it either because the process seems too complicated or they're unsure how best to spend it.

你会惊讶于这笔预算有多少时候被闲置。很多工程师不用它，要么是因为流程看起来太复杂，要么是不确定怎么花才最有价值。

Help demystify it: walk them through the steps, show them how to get approvals, and advocate for carving time out of work to use it.

帮他们破除神秘感：一步步带他们走流程，告诉他们怎么拿到审批，并主动争取从工作中划出时间来使用这笔预算。

Suggest learning options based on their current goals. Conferences, online courses, books, or hands-on learning platforms can all be relevant. Don't limit this to technical domains; make space for things like public speaking, influencing, or writing as well.

根据他们当前的目标推荐学习选项。会议、在线课程、书籍、动手实践平台都可能相关。不要把范围局限在技术领域；也给公开演讲、影响力、写作这类事情留出空间。

Encourage them to work with a coach that can help them reflect, handle feedback better, improve conflict resolution, and work through complex interpersonal situations. It's especially valuable when someone is stepping into a bigger role or facing a major challenge.

鼓励他们请一位教练，帮他们反思、更好地处理反馈、改善冲突解决、并应对复杂的人际局面。尤其当一个人正要承担更大角色或面对重大挑战时，这一点格外有价值。

Make sure these learning activities are considered part of work time. If they're not, advocate for it: negotiate both the budget and the time off needed to attend events or complete learning programs.

确保这些学习活动被算作工作时间。如果不算，就要去争取：既谈预算，也谈参加活动或完成学习项目所需的时间。

— PDF p.332 —

Make learning a shared activity让学习成为共同的活动

Amplify growth by turning individual learning into team momentum.

把个人学习放大为团队动能，从而放大成长。

Book clubs, Slack channels for sharing course notes, or even show-and-tell sessions during retros or team meetings can help normalize learning in your team culture.

读书俱乐部、用来分享课程笔记的 Slack 频道，甚至在复盘会或团队会议上做的展示分享，都有助于让学习在团队文化中变得正常化。

Delegate for development为发展而委派

Delegation is a great growth tool. Chapter 6 explores how to use it effectively. For example, if you always handle a specific design review or infra setup, consider pairing with a team member and handing it off, guiding them while they learn.

委派是一个很好的成长工具。第 6 章探讨了如何有效地使用它。比如，如果你总是亲自处理某个特定的设计评审或基础设施搭建，可以考虑和一位团队成员结对，然后把这件事交出去，在他们学习的过程中引导他们。

Encourage peer or external mentorship鼓励同伴或外部导师

If someone wants to grow in a specific technical or leadership area, help them find a mentor. This could be someone within your company or through a professional mentoring platform.

如果有人想在某个特定技术或领导力领域成长，帮他们找一位导师。可以是公司内部的人，也可以通过专业的导师平台。

Helping someone grow means offering direction, tools, and support while creating space for learning to take root. Your job isn't to do the learning for them but to make it easier for them to move forward with clarity and confidence. Encourage ownership and initiative while also removing friction where you can. With the right structure, your team can take charge of their development and keep making progress.

帮助一个人成长，意味着提供方向、工具和支持，同时为学习扎根创造空间。你的工作不是替他们学习，而是让他们更容易带着清晰和信心往前走。鼓励主人翁意识与主动性，同时在你能做的地方消除阻力。有了合适的结构，你的团队就能掌控自己的发展，并持续取得进步。

Learning Traps to Help Your Team Avoid帮团队避开的学习陷阱

Growth, whether technical or interpersonal, is rarely linear. Even with the right intentions, people often run into common traps that slow or derail progress. As a tech lead, your role is to help people recognize these pitfalls and navigate around them:

成长——无论是技术上还是人际上——很少是线性的。即使出发点是好的，人们也常常会掉进一些常见陷阱，让进展变慢甚至脱轨。作为技术负责人，你的角色是帮大家识别这些陷阱，并绕开它们：

Trap: "There's no time to learn"陷阱："没时间学习"

We're all busy all the time; the real question is this: are we busy with the right things? Learning won't happen unless you make space for it. That means reprioritizing. Some things might need to drop. But if growth is truly important—and it is—there's always a way.

我们所有人一直都很忙；真正的问题是：我们忙的是不是该忙的事？除非你为学习腾出空间，否则学习不会发生。这意味着重新排优先级。有些事情可能要放下。但如果成长真的重要——它确实重要——那总有办法。

Trap: Consuming without applying陷阱：只输入不实践

Sometimes, we find ourselves doing things but not progressing. You can read all the books and take all the courses in the world, but if you don't

有时候，我们发现自己一直在做，却没有进展。你可以读遍世界上所有的书、上完所有的课，但如果你不把学到的东西应用起来，它就留不住。

— PDF p.333 —

apply what you've learned, it doesn't stick. I've seen this loop many times. Encourage your team to turn learning into practice.

我见过这种循环很多次。鼓励你的团队把学习转化为实践。

For example, if someone is learning about systems design, give them ownership of a relevant architectural discussion or RFC.

比如，如果有人正在学习系统设计，就让他主导一次相关的架构讨论或 RFC。

Or, if someone wants to improve their facilitation or communication skills, they could lead a team initiative, facilitate a sprint retro, or represent the team in a cross-functional meeting.

或者，如果有人想提升主持或沟通能力，可以让他牵头一个团队倡议、主持一次迭代复盘，或者在跨职能会议上代表团队发言。

Trap: Learning in isolation from business needs陷阱：学习与业务需求脱节

Learning topics can be disconnected from the team's or business's priorities. Growth should be intentional and useful. Help your team connect what they're learning with what the business actually needs. Encourage your team to ask, "How will this skill contribute to the team/product?" Help connect learning efforts to real outcomes.

学习的主题可能与团队或业务的优先级脱节。成长应该是有意图的、有用的。帮你的团队把所学与业务真正需要的东西连起来。鼓励团队问自己："这项技能将如何为团队/产品做贡献？"帮他们把学习努力与真实成果挂钩。

Trap: Goals that are too big or too many陷阱：目标太大或太多

People often try to fix everything at once. The problem with this trap is that when goals are too big or too numerous, they become overwhelming and demotivating. People either burn out trying to tackle everything at once or fail to start altogether because it feels unmanageable.

人们常常想一下子解决所有问题。这个陷阱的问题在于，当目标太大或太多时，它们会让人感到被压垮、失去动力。人们要么因为想一口气搞定一切而 burnout，要么因为感觉无从下手而根本没开始。

Encourage them to start small and focus on tangible outcomes. For example, instead of aiming for "All my team members give me a lot of useful constructive feedback in the next month," help them redefine it to "One team member gives me one piece of constructive feedback in the next two weeks."

鼓励他们从小处着手，聚焦于可触达的成果。比如，不要把目标定为"下个月所有团队成员都给我大量有用的建设性反馈"，而是帮他们重新定义为"未来两周内，有一位团队成员给我一条建设性反馈"。

Or if the challenge is around decision making, help them go from "Everyone agrees and is happy with the solution" to "We agree on the problem we're trying to solve" or "We move forward even if not everyone agrees, but we have a shared commitment to the decision."

或者，如果挑战是关于决策的，帮他们从"所有人都同意并对方案满意"调整为"我们对要解决的问题达成一致"，或者"即使不是所有人都同意，我们也继续前进，但我们对这个决策有共同承诺"。

Small wins build momentum and confidence.

小胜利积累动能与信心。

Trap: Skipping reflection altogether or relying just on gut feeling to know if they're improving陷阱：完全跳过反思，或只凭直觉判断自己是否在进步

This is one of the most common traps, and it's easy to fall into, especially when you're busy or focused on outcomes. People keep trying new things but without taking a moment to step back and ask, Did that actually work? What impact did it have? Without reflection, there's no clarity, no momentum, and no intentional learning.

这是最常见的陷阱之一，而且很容易掉进去——尤其是当你很忙或专注于结果时。人们不断尝试新做法，却不肯花一点时间退后一步问：那真的有效吗？它带来了什么影响？没有反思，就没有清晰、没有动能、也没有有意识的学习。

— PDF p.334 —

Instead, help your team build a habit of regular reflection and feedback.

相反，要帮团队建立定期反思与反馈的习惯。

For example, since soft skills are all about how we affect others, the best way to understand progress is to ask for input. Encourage your team to request feedback after key moments like meetings, presentations, and decisions, especially when they've tried something new.

比如，既然软技能本质上是关于我们如何影响他人，那么了解进步的最佳方式就是去征求意见。鼓励团队在关键场合——比如会议、演示、决策之后——主动索要反馈，尤其是在他们尝试了新做法之后。

Trap: No accountability陷阱：没有问责机制

Growth takes time and consistency. Without a system of accountability, progress often fades. That's where you come in. Be their accountability partner, or help them find one, whether it's a mentor, a peer, or even a coach. Regular check-ins make learning stick.

成长需要时间和一致性。没有问责机制，进展往往会消退。这就是你发挥作用的地方。做他们的问责伙伴，或者帮他们找一位——无论是导师、同伴，甚至是教练。定期的检查会让学习留存下来。

Growth takes intention. Help your team stay focused, avoid common pitfalls, and keep learning as part of the everyday workflow. Small nudges, regular check-ins, and space to reflect can make all the difference.

成长需要意图。帮团队保持专注、避开常见陷阱、让学习成为日常工作流的一部分。小小的推动、定期的检查、以及反思的空间，都能带来天壤之别。

Managing Stakeholders管理干系人

As a tech lead, your impact doesn't stop at the edge of your team. You also have to manage the relationships that surround your team, the people who influence what gets built, how work gets prioritized, and whether your team's work is truly understood and supported. That's where stakeholder management comes in.

作为技术负责人，你的影响力不止于团队的边界。你还必须管理围绕团队的各种关系——那些影响"做什么"、"工作如何排优先级"、以及"团队的工作是否真正被理解和支持"的人。这就是干系人管理的用武之地。

In this section, I'll explore why managing stakeholders is a core part of your role.

在本节中，我会探讨为什么管理干系人是你这个角色的核心部分。

You'll learn how to identify the right stakeholders, understand what they care about, and build relationships that protect your team and amplify your work.

你将学到如何识别正确的干系人、理解他们关心什么，以及建立那些能保护团队、放大你工作成果的关系。

— PDF p.335 —

From mapping influence to navigating difficult conversations, I'll walk through practical techniques that help you manage these relationships with clarity, empathy, and intent.

从描绘影响力地图，到驾驭困难对话，我会带你走过一系列实用技巧，帮你带着清晰、同理和意图去经营这些关系。

Why You Need to Manage Your Stakeholders为什么你需要管理干系人

As a tech lead, you are the bridge between your team and the rest of the business (Figure 10-1).

作为技术负责人，你是团队与业务其他部分之间的桥梁（图 10-1）。

Stakeholders rely on you. You're their connection to what's happening day-to-day. When things are going well, it's on you to make that visible. When there are risks, blockers, or changes in delivery, you're expected to surface those early

干系人依赖你。你是他们了解日常进展的纽带。一切顺利时，你有责任把顺利呈现出来；当出现风险、阻塞或交付变化时，他们期待你及早把这些摆到台面上，

and clearly explain the impact. This is where your role goes beyond planning and execution; you're also shaping the narrative between what your team is doing and what the business expects.

并清晰地解释影响。在这里，你的角色超越了计划与执行；你也在塑造"团队正在做的事"与"业务所期待的事"之间的叙事。

This part of the role doesn't happen automatically. You can't wait for stakeholders to come to you. Managing stakeholders well takes intention and consistent effort. It starts with building strong relationships, through regular one-on-ones, ongoing updates, and shared systems that make the team's work visible. These relationships should be about building trust, aligning context, and helping stakeholders feel confident in the work being done.

这部分角色不会自动发生。你不能等着干系人来找你。把干系人管理好需要意图和持续的努力。它始于建立稳固的关系——通过定期的一对一、持续的进展更新，以及让团队工作变得可见的共享系统。这些关系的目的是建立信任、对齐上下文，并让干系人对正在进行的工作感到有信心。

Start with your product manager. While both tech leads and product managers engage with stakeholders, their focus differs. PMs typically lead on defining the "what," the product vision, requirements, and prioritization, while tech leads focus on the "how," translating those requirements into feasible plans and identifying technical trade-offs. But this division works only when the partnership is strong. Together, you form the team's core leadership, and how well you collaborate shapes everything from delivery speed to team morale.

从你的产品经理开始。虽然技术负责人和产品经理都会与干系人打交道，但他们的关注点不同。PM 通常主导定义"做什么"——产品愿景、需求和优先级；而技术负责人聚焦"怎么做"——把这些需求转化为可行的计划，并识别技术上的取舍。但这种分工只有在伙伴关系稳固时才成立。你们共同构成团队的核心领导班子，你们协作得如何，会影响从交付速度到团队士气的一切。

— PDF p.336 —

So set up recurring one-on-ones. Align early on how you'll communicate, make trade-offs, and resolve disagreements. When the relationship is healthy, your collaboration brings clarity, consistency, and stability. When it's weak, the team feels the tension, in the form of mixed messages, shifting priorities, or unresolved conflict. Like any partnership, this one takes care and intention. Invest in it.

所以要安排定期的一对一。尽早对齐你们将如何沟通、如何做取舍、如何解决分歧。当关系健康时，你们的协作会带来清晰、一致和稳定；当关系薄弱时，团队会以"信息混乱、优先级漂移、冲突未决"的形式感受到这种张力。和任何伙伴关系一样，这段关系也需要用心和意图。投资在它上面。

And the same goes for your other stakeholders. When these relationships aren't prioritized, misalignment becomes almost inevitable. And when alignment breaks down, execution suffers, no matter how technically solid the work is.

其他干系人也是一样。当这些关系不被优先对待时，错位几乎不可避免。而一旦对齐破裂，无论技术工作多么扎实，执行都会受损。

Almost every month, I hear from a tech lead who's frustrated that their stakeholders are disappointed. Delivery came late, the solution missed the mark, or it wasn't what was expected. And the pattern is often the same: the tech lead focused on execution, assumed alignment, and only brought stakeholders in late, when it was too late to course-correct. These conversations were seen as a distraction from "actual work," when in reality, those conversations are part of the actual work. If you skip early alignment, you might build something technically perfect and still fail.

几乎每个月，我都会听到某位技术负责人抱怨干系人很失望：交付晚了、方案没打中靶心、或者不是他们所期待的样子。模式往往都一样：技术负责人埋头执行、默认已经对齐、直到很晚才把干系人拉进来——那时已经来不及纠偏了。这些对话被看作是对"真正工作"的干扰，而实际上，这些对话本身就是真正工作的一部分。如果你跳过了早期对齐，你可能做出一个技术上完美的东西，却依然失败。

I'll dive into techniques for avoiding this scenario in the upcoming section "Stakeholder Management Techniques" on page 323. But it starts with a mindset shift: managing stakeholder relationships is not separate from your work. It is your work.

我会在第 323 页"干系人管理技巧"一节中详细讲如何避免这种情形。但一切始于心态转变：管理干系人关系不是你工作之外的事情，它就是你的工作。

At the same time, your team needs you to bring information back to them. Stakeholders might change timelines, priorities, or expectations. You need to translate those shifts into clear, actionable guidance. Sometimes that means shielding your team from noise or unrealistic demands. Other times, it means helping them see the bigger picture.

同时，你的团队也需要你把信息带回去。干系人可能会改变时间线、优先级或期望。你需要把这些变化翻译成清晰、可执行的指引。有时这意味着为团队挡住噪音或不切实际的要求；有时则意味着帮他们看到更大的图景。

Let's say you've just learned that a company-wide strategy shift is coming. Your team is mid-way through a six-month plan, but priorities are changing because a key third-party service is increasing prices. The business no longer wants to pay for it and is requesting a migration to a cheaper provider within two months. You now need to go back to the team and develop a plan.

假设你刚得知公司层面的战略要变。你的团队正在进行一个为期六个月的计划，但因为一个关键第三方服务要涨价，优先级变了。业务不再愿意为它付钱，要求在两个月内迁移到更便宜的供应商。你现在需要回到团队，拿出一个计划。

They won't like the news, and how you deliver it will determine how they respond. If you can explain why the change is happening, share the reason behind the tight timeline, propose an alternative provider, and secure stakeholder buy-in to adjust the scope up front, your team is more likely to get on board.

他们不会喜欢这个消息，而你传递消息的方式将决定他们如何回应。如果你能解释为什么会发生这个变化、分享紧凑时间线背后的原因、提出一个替代供应商，并事先争取到干系人同意调整范围，你的团队就更可能接受它。

— PDF p.337 —

Anticipating their questions—Why this change? Why now? Will this mean extra hours?—allows you to lead with clarity and empathy.

预判他们的问题——为什么要变？为什么是现在？这意味着要加班吗？——能让你带着清晰和同理去引导。

You don't need to have all the answers before talking to your team. You'll make the plan together. But the more context you gather ahead of time, the smoother that conversation will be. Go in with the attitude of "I know this isn't ideal, and I need your help to figure it out," rather than "This is what we're doing."

在和团队谈话之前，你不必拥有所有答案。你们会一起制定计划。但你提前收集的上下文越多，对话就会越顺畅。带着这样的态度进去："我知道这不理想，我需要你们帮我一起想办法"，而不是"我们就这么干"。

Finding that balance—being the translator, the advocate, and the filter—is what makes this part of the role so critical.

找到那种平衡——做翻译者、倡导者和过滤器——正是这部分角色之所以关键的原因。

It's also important to continuously keep in mind that relationships are always two-way. Just as stakeholders are essential to your team's success, your team is essential to theirs, and they know it. This means you shouldn't view stakeholders only as people in charge or gatekeepers but as allies who share a common goal. Ask for their help when you need it. If there's a blocker, ask them to use their influence to help clear the way. If a decision needs broader buy-in, ask them to support you in championing your proposal. They're not just there to be managed; they're there to help, too. It's in both your interests to succeed. Frame the relationship as a partnership rather than a hierarchy.

同样重要的是，要持续记住：关系永远是双向的。正如干系人对团队的成功不可或缺，你的团队对他们的成功也不可或缺——而他们知道这一点。这意味着你不应只把干系人看作掌权者或守门人，而应看作共享同一目标的盟友。需要时就请他们帮忙。如果有阻塞，请他们用影响力帮你扫清道路。如果一个决策需要更广泛的支持，请他们支持你去为提案站台。他们不只是在那里等你去"管理"；他们也在那里提供帮助。你们双方的利益都在于成功。把这段关系框定为伙伴关系，而不是层级关系。

I know it can be frustrating, but success isn't just about what you deliver; it's about what's recognized. You could build the most technically impressive product in the company, but if no one knows about it, it doesn't move the needle. Like it or not, marketing matters. It's your job to make your team's impact visible by tying outcomes to business value and communicating in ways stakeholders will hear and understand.

我知道这可能让人沮丧，但成功不只是关于你交付了什么；它还关于什么被看见了。你可以做出全公司技术上最令人惊叹的产品，但如果没人知道它，它就不会带来任何改变。不管你喜不喜欢，营销很重要。你的工作就是把成果与业务价值挂钩，用干系人听得进、听得懂的方式沟通，让团队的影响力被看见。

Managing stakeholders is one of the core ways you create impact as a tech lead. Do it well, and your team will have the clarity, trust, and support it needs to thrive.

管理干系人是你作为技术负责人创造影响力的核心方式之一。做好了，你的团队就会拥有绽放所需的清晰、信任和支持。

Identifying Your Stakeholders识别你的干系人

As the tech lead, you are the voice and shield of your team. You're the one with the full context of what the team is building, how they're working, and what challenges they face. It's your job to represent the team's needs and interests with clarity and accuracy, to shield the team from distractions or misaligned external pressures.

作为技术负责人，你是团队的传声筒和盾牌。你是那个掌握完整上下文的人：团队在构建什么、他们如何工作、他们面临什么挑战。你的工作是清晰而准确地代表团队的需求和利益，为团队挡住干扰或错位的外部压力。

— PDF p.338 —

To effectively represent your team, you need a clear view of the larger organizational context. You need to understand how the company is structured, who holds decision-making power, who controls resources, and who might be unexpectedly relevant.

要有效地代表团队，你需要对更大的组织上下文有清晰的认识。你需要理解公司是怎么架构的、谁掌握决策权、谁控制资源，以及谁可能出乎意料地相关。

A great way to begin this process is by reviewing any available documentation on your company's organizational structure. Many companies maintain visible org charts outlining roles and hierarchies.

开始这个过程的一个好办法，是查阅公司组织架构的任何现有文档。很多公司都会维护可见的组织架构图，勾勒出角色和层级。

If this structure doesn't exist, create your own. Start by listing everyone who might influence your team's work. Stakeholders exist at multiple levels, not just senior leader or formal roles. Consider collaborators from across the organization, such as product managers, designers, QA, infrastructure, and security teams, as well as adjacent product teams with shared dependencies.

如果这种结构不存在，就自己建一个。先列出所有可能影响团队工作的人。干系人存在于多个层级，而不仅仅是高级领导或正式角色。考虑整个组织中的协作者，比如产品经理、设计师、QA、基础设施、安全团队，以及有共享依赖的相邻产品团队。

Also be aware of informal influence. Influence isn't always tied to job titles. Some people shape direction through relationships, expertise, or institutional knowledge. Think of long-tenured engineers, well-connected peers, or customer-facing staff who engage regularly with users. For example, there is often a developer who's been with the company for a long time—maybe even from the beginning—or someone who built a core part of the product. Even without a formal leadership title, people look to these people for guidance and opinions. That's definitely someone to add to your stakeholder list.

也要留意非正式影响力。影响力并不总是与职位头衔挂钩。有些人通过关系、专长或机构知识来塑造方向。想想那些长任期的工程师、人脉广的同伴，或者经常与用户打交道的一线人员。比如，公司里常常有一位加入很久——也许甚至从一开始就在——的开发者，或者某个构建了产品核心部分的人。即使没有正式的领导头衔，人们也会向这些人寻求指引和意见。这个人绝对应该加到你的干系人名单里。

Pay attention to who others defer to in meetings, who helps resolve cross-team issues, or who consistently brings hidden context to light. These individuals may not appear on an org chart as decision makers, but their impact is real and often significant. Including them in your stakeholder strategy can make the difference between reactive firefighting and proactive alignment.

留意在会议上别人会顺从谁、谁帮助解决跨团队问题、谁总是能把隐藏的上下文带到台面上。这些人可能不会作为决策者出现在组织架构图上，但他们的影响是真实的，而且往往很重要。把他们纳入你的干系人策略，可能就是"被动救火"与"主动对齐"之间的差别。

As you build this list, consider the following questions:

在构建这份名单时，思考下面这些问题：

  • Who can significantly affect my team's ability to succeed?谁能显著影响我团队成功的能力？
  • Who could amplify our success if I had a stronger relationship with them?如果我和谁的关系更强，谁就能放大我们的成功？
  • Who is currently making decisions that affect my team, even indirectly?谁目前正在做影响我团队的决策，哪怕是间接的？
  • Who holds information, context, or resources that could help us succeed?谁掌握着能帮我们成功的信息、上下文或资源？
  • Who might block our work, intentionally or not, if we don't engage them early?如果我们不早期接触谁，谁可能有意或无意地阻碍我们的工作？
  • Who has a vested interest in the outcomes we are working toward?谁对我们正在努力达成的结果有既得利益？
— PDF p.339 —

These questions will help you identify which relationships to invest in and guide your strategy for building and managing stakeholder connections.

这些问题会帮你识别应该投资哪些关系，并指导你建立和管理干系人连接的策略。

If you're uncertain about who truly holds influence or how decisions are made, talk to people. Short, informal one-on-one conversations can be incredibly revealing. Ask questions like "Who else should I be talking to?" or "Who influences decisions around this area?"

如果你不确定谁真正掌握影响力、决策是如何做出的，就去找人聊。简短、非正式的一对一对话可能极其有启发性。问类似这样的问题："我还应该和谁聊聊？"或者"谁在影响这个领域的决策？"

As you uncover more about your stakeholders, consider documenting these insights. Keep a lightweight, private record that captures who your key players are, what they care about, how they prefer to communicate, and any notable context or risks. Such a resource becomes especially valuable when onboarding new leads, sharing knowledge with peers, or navigating shifting team dynamics.

随着你对干系人了解越多，考虑把这些洞见记录下来。保存一份轻量、私密的记录，记下你的关键人物是谁、他们关心什么、他们偏好如何沟通，以及任何值得注意的上下文或风险。这样一份资料在带新负责人入职、与同伴共享知识或应对团队动态变化时会格外有价值。

One common tool for visualizing your stakeholders is the Mendelow Power-Interest Matrix, which helps you map stakeholders based on how much power they hold and how much interest they have in your team's work. It's a simple way to guide your engagement strategy—who to involve closely, who to keep satisfied, and who just needs occasional updates.

一个常用的干系人可视化工具是 Mendelow 权力-利益矩阵，它根据干系人拥有多大权力、对你团队的工作有多大兴趣来绘制他们的位置。这是一个简单的方式来指导你的参与策略——谁要密切参与、谁要保持满意、谁只需要偶尔更新。

Another useful tool, and the one I'll explore in the next section, is the stakeholders map. It uses a straightforward two-axis framework: one axis for influence (meaning how much they can impact your team) and one for commitment or alignment (whether they are a supporter or a detractor).

另一个有用的工具——也是我下一节要展开的——是干系人地图。它使用一个简单的两轴框架：一个轴是影响力（即他们能在多大程度上影响你的团队），另一个轴是承诺度或对齐度（他们是支持者还是反对者）。

Intent also exists on a spectrum. Supporters believe in your goals and work with you to achieve them. They are your partners in success. Detractors may not yet believe in your work or might even oppose it. Often, this opposition is not personal; it may come from broader organizational dynamics or differing priorities.

意图也存在于一个光谱上。支持者相信你的目标，并与你一起实现它。他们是你成功路上的伙伴。反对者可能还不相信你的工作，甚至可能反对它。通常，这种反对不是针对个人的；它可能来自更广泛的组织动态或不同的优先级。

Stakeholder Management Techniques干系人管理技巧

Now that you have your stakeholders mapped out, it's time to put that map to use. The goal here is to tailor your engagement strategy based on where each stakeholder sits in terms of their influence and commitment.

现在你已经把干系人画在了地图上，是时候把这张地图用起来了。这里的目标是根据每个干系人在影响力和承诺度上的位置，来定制你的参与策略。

The map (Figure 10-2) gives you a clear picture of where to focus your attention.

这张地图（图 10-2）让你清楚看到应该把注意力聚焦在哪里。

— PDF p.340 —

Stakeholders generally fall into four categories:

干系人通常分为四类：

  • High-influence detractors are critical to manage closely. These individuals can block or derail progress if not engaged carefully. Understanding their concerns and working to build alignment is essential.高影响力反对者：必须密切管理。如果不小心应对，这些人可能阻塞或让进展脱轨。理解他们的顾虑、努力建立对齐至关重要。
  • High-influence supporters are your champions. Keep them happy, informed, aligned, and engaged. Their advocacy is powerful.高影响力支持者：是你的拥护者。让他们满意、知情、对齐、投入。他们的背书非常有力量。
  • Low-influence detractors should be monitored. They don't require heavy investment unless their influence grows.低影响力反对者：保持监控。除非他们的影响力增长，否则不需要重投入。
  • Low-influence supporters should be kept in the loop. They may grow in influence or help provide useful context and feedback.低影响力支持者：保持信息同步。他们的影响力可能增长，也可能帮你提供有用的上下文和反馈。

Empathy is key同理心是关键

Empathy is key, especially when working with detractors. What's driving their perspective? Are they under pressure themselves? What do they want to see happen?

同理心是关键，尤其是在与反对者打交道时。是什么在驱动他们的视角？他们自己也在承受压力吗？他们想看到什么结果？

For example, while working in a consultancy, we were preparing to roll off a client project and needed to hand over our work to their internal team. We proposed pairing on tasks, a method we believed would transfer knowledge quickly while still delivering value. But an engineering leader on the client side was

比如，在一家咨询公司工作时，我们准备从一个客户项目撤出，需要把工作交接给他们的内部团队。我们提议在任务上结对，我们相信这种方法既能快速传递知识、又能持续交付价值。但客户方的一位工程负责人强烈反对。

— PDF p.341 —

strongly against it. Despite offering every rationale—speed, quality, continuity—he wouldn't budge.

尽管我们提出了所有理由——速度、质量、连续性——他就是不让步。

So I teamed up with the account manager and scheduled a call with him. We didn't try to convince him again. Instead, we listened. He shared concerns based on past experiences: handovers had taken too long, the team lacked experience, and remote collaboration tools weren't ideal. He was also nervous about how the change would land with his team.

于是我和客户经理组队，约了他一次电话。我们没有再试图说服他，而是倾听。他分享了基于过去经历的顾虑：交接过去耗时太长、团队缺乏经验、远程协作工具不理想。他也担心这个变化在他的团队里会怎样落地。

Only after fully hearing him out did we respond. At this point he seemed way more open to conversation. We explained how we planned to address those concerns: checking in with his engineers to ensure they were also on board, building a lightweight plan with clear support, and committing to a short trial period to see how it went. He agreed to those actions.

在完整听完他之后我们才回应。这时他看起来对谈话开放多了。我们解释了计划如何应对这些顾虑：与他的工程师确认他们也认同、制定一个带清晰支持的轻量计划、并承诺一个短期试用期看看效果。他同意了这些做法。

The team got on board, and the pairing experiment worked surprisingly well. We kept him in the loop at every stage, shared updates, and encouraged feedback from the engineers on the ground. By the end of two weeks, he was all in for pairing as a handover approach.

团队接受了，结对实验效果出奇地好。我们每个阶段都让他知情、分享进展，并鼓励一线工程师反馈。两周结束时，他已经完全支持把结对作为一种交接方式。

That experience taught me that when resistance shows up, your first job is to understand. Behind most pushback is a story: a past experience, a pressure, a concern that hasn't been voiced yet. Once we acknowledged his concerns, reflected them back, and offered a low-risk way to move forward, trust started to build.

那次经历教会我，当阻力出现时，你的第一要务是理解。大多数反对背后都有一个故事：一段过去的经历、一种压力、一个尚未说出口的顾虑。一旦我们承认他的顾虑、把它们复述回去、并提供一条低风险的前进路径，信任就开始建立了。

Sometimes, people just need to feel heard before they can move forward. Other times, they need help navigating internal optics, such as how a decision might reflect on them within their own team. Being mindful of that, and helping them look good in front of their peers, can make all the difference.

有时候，人们只是需要在前进之前感到自己被听见。另一些时候，他们需要你帮助应对内部观感——比如一个决策在他们自己团队中会如何反映到他们身上。留心这一点，并帮他们在同伴面前表现出色，可能就会带来天壤之别。

And sometimes, the most powerful thing you can do is remind them that you're on the same side. Reassure them that you care about finding a solution that works for everyone. Simple phrases like "I want to make this work for all of us" or "I need your help to figure this out" can lower defensiveness and invite collaboration.

还有时候，你能做的最有力量的事，是提醒他们：你们站在同一边。让他们安心：你关心的是找到一个对所有人都行得通的方案。像"我想让这件事对我们所有人都好"或"我需要你的帮助来想清楚这件事"这样简单的话，就能降低防御、邀请协作。

In the end, empathy turned that blocker into a collaborator. That's the power of showing up curious instead of defensive. And it's one of the most valuable tools you have in stakeholder management.

最终，同理心把那个阻碍者变成了协作者。这就是带着好奇心、而不是防御心出现的力量。这也是你在干系人管理中最有价值的工具之一。

Adapt your communication style调整你的沟通风格

A big part of stakeholder alignment comes down to communication. One helpful framework for adapting your style to theirs is the DISC model, originally

干系人对齐很大程度上归结于沟通。一个帮你根据对方风格调整自己的有用框架是 DISC 模型，它最初

— PDF p.342 —

developed by psychologist William Moulton Marston, which classifies behavior into four primary styles (Figure 10-3):

由心理学家 William Moulton Marston 提出，把行为分为四种主要风格（图 10-3）：

  • Dominance (D): Results-focused, assertive, challenge-driven.支配型（D）：结果导向、果断、以挑战为驱动。
  • Influence (I): People-oriented, enthusiastic, social.影响型（I）：以人为导向、热情、爱社交。
  • Steadiness (S): Calm, consistent, team-oriented.稳健型（S）：冷静、稳定、团队导向。
  • Conscientiousness (C): Precise, analytical, data-driven.谨慎型（C）：精确、分析型、数据驱动。

Understanding where your stakeholder falls on this spectrum helps you communicate more effectively:

理解你的干系人落在这个光谱的哪里，能帮你更有效地沟通：

— PDF p.343 —
  • For D styles, be direct and focus on solutions. Let them make decisions.对 D 型：直接、聚焦解决方案。让他们做决定。
  • For I styles, engage with enthusiasm, share stories, and allow them to ask questions.对 I 型：热情地互动、分享故事、允许他们提问。
  • For S styles, be personal and friendly, give them time to process, and avoid confrontation.对 S 型：亲切友好，给他们时间消化，避免正面冲突。
  • For C styles, stick to facts, reduce emotional language, and allow time for them to process the information before giving a response.对 C 型：紧扣事实，减少情绪化语言，在给出回应之前给他们时间消化信息。

It's equally important to understand your own default communication tendencies and how they might clash with others. DISC styles that sit opposite each other on the spectrum tend to experience the most friction.

同样重要的是理解你自己默认的沟通倾向，以及它们可能如何与他人冲突。在光谱上相对的两种 DISC 风格，往往会经历最多的摩擦。

For example, I naturally fall into the C (conscientiousness) style; I like structure, precision, and thoughtful communication. But I've struggled at times when working with I (influence) stakeholders. Their fast pace, high energy, and preference for informal, emotional connection can feel overwhelming or vague to me. Meanwhile, they may find my style too rigid or cautious.

比如，我天生属于 C（谨慎）型；我喜欢结构、精确和深思熟虑的沟通。但在与 I（影响）型干系人合作时，我有时会很吃力。他们快节奏、高能量、偏好非正式和情感连接的风格，对我来说可能让人招架不住或感觉模糊。而他们可能觉得我的风格太僵化或太谨慎。

Recognizing these gaps has helped me adjust. With I styles, I've learned to loosen up, speak more casually, and share more personal context. That small shift in tone often opens the door to stronger connection and trust.

识别这些差距帮我做出了调整。面对 I 型，我学会了放松、说话更随意、分享更多个人上下文。语气上那一小点转变，往往就能为更强的连接和信任打开大门。

Adjusting your style means being intentional about how you show up so you can be heard instead of ignored.

调整你的风格，意味着有意识地决定你以什么样子出现，好让自己被听见，而不是被忽略。

Build trust over time随时间建立信任

Adapting your style is one way to build trust, but nothing beats the kind that comes from time and consistency. That's why my favorite strategy for stakeholder management is building trust over time. It's not always possible; some environments move too fast or change too often for deep relationships to form. It requires continuity and time spent working closely with the same stakeholders. But if you do get that opportunity, take it. The payoff is worth every bit of effort.

调整风格是建立信任的一种方式，但没有什么比来自时间和一致性的信任更有力量。这就是为什么我最喜欢的干系人管理策略是随时间建立信任。它并不总是可行；有些环境变化太快、太频繁，深关系无法形成。它需要连续性，需要与同一批干系人紧密合作的时间。但如果你真的得到这种机会，抓住它。回报值得每一分努力。

I was lucky to be in environments where this kind of consistency was possible—same team, same stakeholders over a long stretch of time. That stability made it easier to invest in strong relationships and see the benefits. I encountered relatively little resistance because trust was already there. When my team had to make a tough technical call that delayed delivery, the stakeholder's response was simply "If you say it's needed, it's needed. I trust you." That kind of response is earned through how you consistently show up.

我很幸运曾身处这种一致性成为可能的环境——长时间里同一支团队、同一批干系人。那种稳定性让投资于稳固关系变得更容易，也让回报可见。我遇到的阻力相对较少，因为信任已经在了。当我的团队不得不做出一个会延迟交付的艰难技术决策时，干系人的回应很简单："如果你说需要，那就需要。我相信你。"这种回应是靠你一贯的表现挣来的。

If you're in a stable context, I highly recommend applying the principles from the section "How to Build Strong Relationships" on page 62. Focus on consistent and transparent communication: hold recurring one-on-ones with stakeholders, go beyond just sharing updates, communicate risks early, seek and

如果你处在一个稳定的环境，我强烈建议应用第 62 页"如何建立稳固关系"一节中的原则。聚焦于持续、透明的沟通：与干系人举行定期一对一，不只是分享进展，还要及早沟通风险、寻求并

— PDF p.344 —

incorporate feedback, and most importantly, follow through on your promises. Delivering consistently builds credibility.

吸纳反馈；最重要的是，兑现你的承诺。持续交付会建立信誉。

Strong collaboration comes from trust, consistency, and shared ownership.

稳固的协作来自信任、一致性和共同拥有。

So when you do get the chance to invest in long-term relationships, make it count. They'll pay off far beyond any single project.

所以，当你真的得到投资于长期关系的机会时，让它值得。它们的回报会远远超过任何单个项目。

A powerful but often overlooked tip: involve your team in the process of building stakeholder relationships. Teach your team members why these relationships matter and how to build them. For example, if you have a feature lead running an initiative that depends on close collaboration with another team, encourage them to set up recurring one-on-ones with the lead on the other team, create shared communication rituals, and celebrate wins together. When more people on your team build strong relationships across the organization, your collective impact grows, and so does yours, by extension.

一个有力却常被忽略的建议：让你的团队参与建立干系人关系的过程。教你的团队成员这些关系为什么重要、如何建立它们。比如，如果你有一位功能负责人正在牵头一项需要与另一团队紧密协作的倡议，鼓励他与对方团队的负责人建立定期一对一、创建共享的沟通仪式、并一起庆祝胜利。当你团队里更多人在整个组织内建立稳固关系时，你们的集体影响力会增长，你个人的影响力也会随之放大。

Bringing it all together: A lightweight framework融会贯通：一个轻量框架

To make these strategies easier to remember and apply, I use a lightweight framework I call the 3Rs of stakeholder alignment:

为了让这些策略更容易记住和应用，我使用一个轻量框架，我称之为干系人对齐的 3R：

  • Reframe: Translate technical needs into business value.重构（Reframe）：把技术需求翻译为业务价值。
  • Relate: Connect the work to stakeholder goals and priorities.关联（Relate）：把工作与干系人的目标和优先级连起来。
  • Reinforce: Share progress and outcomes consistently to build confidence.强化（Reinforce）：持续分享进展与成果，建立信心。

This lightweight mental model can serve as a quick checkpoint anytime you prepare to engage stakeholders about a decision.

这个轻量心智模型，可以在任何你准备就一个决策与干系人沟通时，作为一个快速检查点。

Stakeholder alignment is about building trust, finding common ground, and creating momentum together. Like any leadership skill, it gets stronger with practice, reflection, and consistency. The more you invest in these relationships, the easier it becomes to navigate complexity.

干系人对齐关乎建立信任、寻找共同点、并共同创造动能。和任何领导力技能一样，它会随着练习、反思和一致性而变强。你在这些关系上投资越多，驾驭复杂就越容易。

Common Challenges in Navigating Technical Leadership驾驭技术领导力中的常见挑战

Even experienced tech leads can struggle with the realities of the role as it requires navigating an environment full of competing priorities, shifting expectations, and limited time. This section explores some of the most common (and often unspoken) challenges you'll face in the day-to-day of technical leadership.

即使是经验丰富的技术负责人，也可能在这个角色的现实面前感到吃力——因为它要求你在一个充满相互竞争的优先级、不断变化的期望和有限时间的环境中前行。本节探讨你在技术领导力日常中会面对的一些最常见（且往往不言自明）的挑战。

— PDF p.345 —

I'll look at how to secure stakeholder buy-in for technical initiatives, especially when the value isn't immediately visible. I'll also explore how to measure your own success in a role that often lacks clear metrics. And finally, I'll confront the emotional and mental toll of trying to do it all, and what it really takes to lead without burning out.

我会探讨如何为技术倡议争取干系人支持——尤其是当价值不能立刻被看见时。我也会探讨，在一个常常缺乏清晰指标的角色中，如何衡量你自己的成功。最后，我会直面"什么都想做"带来的情绪与心理代价，以及如何在不 burnout 的前提下真正当好领导。

Getting Stakeholder Buy-In on Technical Topics在技术议题上争取干系人支持

Securing time from stakeholders to focus on technical topics often proves challenging for tech leads. Whether it's addressing tech debt, resolving deep system issues like memory leaks, or improving internal tools for better development workflows, advocating for technical work can often feel like an uphill battle.

为技术议题争取干系人的时间，对技术负责人来说往往很有挑战。无论是处理技术债、解决像内存泄漏这样的深层系统问题，还是改进内部工具以优化开发工作流，为技术工作发声常常感觉像一场爬坡战。

The core problem is that many tech leads approach these conversations like a confrontation. They brace for resistance and forget a crucial truth: stakeholders and engineers are on the same side. They all want the same outcome: successful delivery and sustainable progress.

核心问题在于，很多技术负责人把这些对话当成对抗来准备。他们做好了迎接阻力的准备，却忘了一个关键事实：干系人和工程师站在同一边。他们都想要同一个结果：成功的交付和可持续的进展。

Often, when stakeholders don't give their buy-in, it's not because they're against the work; it's because they don't fully understand the value, urgency, or impact. The misalignment in priorities and language can make technical work seem abstract, low priority, or disconnected from business goals. The key is finding that common ground, and that's where the 3Rs of stakeholder alignment comes in (described in the section "Stakeholder Management Techniques" on page 323).

通常，干系人不支持，不是因为他们反对这项工作；而是因为他们没有完全理解其价值、紧迫性或影响。优先级和语言上的错位，会让技术工作显得抽象、低优先级、或与业务目标脱节。关键是找到那个共同点，而这正是干系人对齐 3R 框架的用武之地（见第 323 页"干系人管理技巧"一节）。

Here's the framework applied to some of the most common technical topics tech leads need to advocate for:

下面把这个框架应用到技术负责人最常需要为之发声的一些技术议题上：

Addressing an underlying system issue处理一个底层系统问题

One memorable example for me was a persistent memory leak in one of our most critical services, built on .NET. Initially, the problem appeared minor: the service would occasionally stop responding. Restarting the servers fixed it temporarily, so that became our short-term workaround. We were busy launching a new project, and this recurring issue kept getting pushed aside. Eventually, a new team member joined and asked the hard question "Why is this happening again and again?," so we could no longer ignore it.

一个让我印象深刻的例子，是我们一个最关键服务中顽固的内存泄漏，该服务基于 .NET。起初问题看起来不大：服务偶尔会停止响应。重启服务器能临时修好，于是那成了我们的短期权宜之计。当时我们正忙于上线一个新项目，这个反复出现的问题一再被搁置。最终，一位新团队成员加入，问出了那个尖锐的问题："为什么这件事一再发生？"于是我们再也不能忽视它。

We proposed a one-day spike to investigate, which quickly uncovered a serious memory leak. Fixing it wasn't going to be fast, and it wasn't something we could afford to ignore either. I needed product buy-in to dedicate the time.

我们提议用一天时间做一个 spike（探针式调研），很快就发现了一处严重的内存泄漏。修复它不会很快，但我们也承担不起忽视它的代价。我需要产品方同意投入时间。

— PDF p.346 —

I got that buy-in by applying the 3Rs of stakeholder alignment framework:

我通过应用干系人对齐 3R 框架获得了支持：

  • Reframe: I explained what the memory leak meant, not just for the business: increased infrastructure costs, service downtime, and poor user experience.重构（Reframe）：我解释了内存泄漏意味着什么——不只是技术上的，而是对业务：基础设施成本上升、服务宕机、以及糟糕的用户体验。
  • Relate: I tied the issue to broader stakeholder concerns, including customer impact and potential long-term delays.关联（Relate）：我把这个问题与干系人更广泛的顾虑挂钩，包括对客户的影响和潜在的长期延迟。
  • Reinforce: I committed to providing regular updates via standups and sprint reviews, which helped maintain transparency and confidence.强化（Reinforce）：我承诺通过站会和迭代评审提供定期更新，这有助于保持透明度和信心。

Once the issue was fixed, the job wasn't over. We measured and shared the impact: how much time was saved, how reliability improved, and how morale lifted. Mentioning these results in retros and sprint reviews helped stakeholders see the return on their investment.

问题修好之后，工作并没有结束。我们衡量并分享了影响：节省了多少时间、可靠性提升了多少、士气提升了多少。在复盘和迭代评审中提到这些结果，帮干系人看到了他们投资的回报。

Advocating for a major refactoring为大型重构发声

A common situation many tech leads face is advocating for a major refactoring of a legacy system. From the outside, the system may appear stable, but internally it's brittle, difficult to maintain, and slows down the team's ability to ship new features with confidence.

很多技术负责人都会面对的一个常见情境，是为遗留系统的大型重构发声。从外面看，系统可能显得稳定，但内部它脆弱、难以维护，并拖慢团队有信心地交付新功能的能力。

To secure stakeholder buy-in for a large refactor, you can apply the 3Rs of stakeholder alignment:

要为大型重构争取干系人支持，你可以应用干系人对齐 3R：

  • Reframe: Explain that while the system is still functional, it's causing delivery slowdowns and increasing the likelihood of bugs. Position the refactoring not as internal cleanup but as an investment to speed up feature development and reduce long-term risk.重构（Reframe）：解释虽然系统还能跑，但它正在拖慢交付、增加 bug 概率。把重构定位为投资，而不是内部大扫除——它会加速功能开发、降低长期风险。
  • Relate: Connect the challenges your team is facing with recent stakeholder pain, like missed deadlines, escalating QA time, or inability to capitalize on new business opportunities. Be explicit about timelines and impact: propose a clear plan that outlines how the refactor affects the current roadmap and how you're mitigating disruption.关联（Relate）：把团队正在面对的挑战，与干系人最近的痛点连起来——比如错过截止日期、QA 时间不断上升、或无法抓住新业务机会。在时间线和影响上要明确：提出一个清晰计划，勾勒重构如何影响当前路线图、以及你将如何减轻扰动。
— PDF p.347 —
  • A piece of advice here: steer clear of proposing a months-long "let's stop everything and rewrite the whole thing" plan. The cost and business risk are too high, and your stakeholders will rightfully push back on pausing product progress for months. Instead, look for ways to break down the work, tackle it incrementally, and continue delivering value throughout.这里有一条建议：避免提出那种长达数月的"让我们停下一切、重写整个东西"的计划。成本和业务风险都太高，干系人会理所当然地拒绝让产品进展暂停数月。相反，想办法把工作拆小、增量地处理，并在整个过程中持续交付价值。
  • Reinforce: Commit to visibility. Share progress through sprint reviews or status updates, and highlight the gains with before-and-after comparisons.强化（Reinforce）：承诺透明度。通过迭代评审或状态更新分享进展，并用前后对比来突出收益。

Dealing with tech debt处理技术债

You can find the 3Rs of stakeholder alignment framework applied to advocating for tech debt in the section "Managing Technical Debt" on page 249.

你可以在第 249 页"管理技术债"一节中，看到干系人对齐 3R 框架如何应用于为技术债发声。

Getting stakeholder buy-in on technical topics doesn't have to be a battle. When you apply the 3 Rs—reframe, relate, and reinforce—you shift the conversation from resistance to collaboration.

在技术议题上争取干系人支持，不必是一场战斗。当你应用这三个 R——重构、关联、强化——你就把对话从"对抗"转向了"协作"。

Of course, buy-in doesn't always mean getting everything you ask for. Sometimes it involves negotiation, compromise, or finding middle ground, perhaps reducing the scope, tying the work to a business milestone, or deferring part of it. These trade-offs are a normal and necessary part of the process. Just as important is knowing when to push and when to let go.

当然，获得支持并不总是意味着你要什么就得到什么。有时它涉及谈判、妥协或寻找中间地带——也许缩小范围、把工作绑定到一个业务里程碑上，或者把一部分推迟。这些取舍是过程中正常且必要的一部分。同样重要的是知道什么时候该坚持、什么时候该放手。

For example, you might propose rebuilding a fragile internal tool, but your stakeholders push back due to an upcoming product launch. Rather than insisting on doing it all at once, you apply a negotiation mindset and look for mutual gain. You agree to reduce the scope and focus on just the most unstable part of the tool now, which helps avoid potential outages during the launch, and defer the rest to a quieter release window.

比如，你可能提议重建一个脆弱的内部工具，但干系人因为即将到来的产品上线而反对。你不要坚持一次性做完，而是运用谈判思维寻找互利。你同意缩小范围、现在只聚焦工具中最不稳定的部分——这有助于避免上线期间可能发生的宕机——其余部分推迟到一个更安静的发布窗口。

Even if you do everything right, sometimes it just doesn't go your way. You might communicate clearly, align goals, and build trust, and still hear "no." For example, you might propose introducing automated performance testing to catch regressions early. But stakeholders decline because they don't see an immediate need, especially with a major product launch approaching. Rather than walking away frustrated, you follow up to understand the reasoning. You learn their concern is about adding complexity during a high-stakes window.

即使你做对了所有事，有时事情还是不遂愿。你可能沟通得很清楚、对齐了目标、建立了信任，却仍然听到"不"。比如，你可能提议引入自动化性能测试以尽早发现回归。但干系人拒绝了，因为他们看不到即时需求——尤其在重大产品上线临近时。你不要带着挫败走开，而是跟进去理解原因。你了解到他们的顾虑是：在一个高风险窗口期间增加复杂性。

Instead of forcing the issue, you agree to revisit the proposal after the launch. In the meantime, you begin collecting examples where performance regressions slipped through unnoticed, helping to build a stronger case for the

你不要强推这件事，而是同意在上线之后重新讨论这个提案。与此同时，你开始收集那些性能回归在没人注意的情况下溜过去的例子，为未来构建更有力的论据。

— PDF p.348 —

future. This approach keeps the relationship intact, demonstrates patience and strategic thinking, and lays the groundwork for future buy-in.

这种方式保持了关系完好，展现了耐心和战略思维，并为未来的支持铺好了路。

With these strategies in place, you can advocate effectively for your team's needs while keeping stakeholders engaged and supportive.

有了这些策略，你就能有效地为团队的需求发声，同时让干系人保持参与和支持。

As a next step, reflect on this: what's one technical priority your team needs stakeholder support for right now? How could you reframe it in terms of business value? Who do you need to start building a relationship with today to make that conversation easier tomorrow?

作为下一步，反思一下：你们团队现在最需要干系人支持的一个技术优先级是什么？你如何用业务价值的语言重新框定它？你今天需要开始和谁建立关系，好让明天的那场对话更容易？

Measuring Success in Technical Leadership衡量技术领导力中的成功

Success in technical leadership isn't as clear-cut as shipping features or fixing bugs. It's about influence, alignment, and long-term impact: things that don't show up in commit histories or sprint velocity charts. And that makes it incredibly hard to measure.

技术领导力中的成功，不像交付功能或修 bug 那样清晰。它关乎影响力、对齐和长期影响——这些东西不会出现在提交历史或迭代速度图上。而这让它极其难以衡量。

As a tech lead, your role sits in a blurry middle ground: not quite management, not purely an individual contributor. You guide architecture, support delivery, grow team members, and bridge communication between technical and nontechnical teams. But there's often no formal rubric that tells you how well you're doing.

作为技术负责人，你的角色处在一个模糊的中间地带：既不完全是管理，也不纯粹是个人贡献者。你指导架构、支持交付、培养团队成员、并在技术与非技术团队之间搭建沟通桥梁。但通常没有一份正式评分标准告诉你做得怎么样。

That's what makes this so tricky: you're expected to lead but rarely told how success will be judged. And when there's no clear feedback loop, many tech leads start to second-guess themselves. They wonder if they're doing enough. Or worse, if their contributions even count.

这就是这件事棘手的原因：你被期待去领导，却很少有人告诉你成功将如何被评判。而当没有清晰的反馈回路时，很多技术负责人开始自我怀疑。他们想知道自己做得够不够。或者更糟，怀疑自己的贡献到底算不算数。

The ambiguity leads to a lot of quiet frustration. Performance evaluations may still rely on outdated metrics like lines of code, Jira tickets closed, or how "busy" you appear. These don't reflect the real, valuable work of unblocking others, maintaining technical quality under pressure, or shaping a healthy engineering culture.

这种模糊性导致了大量无声的挫败。绩效评估可能仍然依赖过时的指标——代码行数、关闭的 Jira 工单、或者你看起来有多"忙"。这些都无法反映那些真正有价值的工作：为他人解除阻塞、在压力下维护技术质量、或塑造健康的工程文化。

Meanwhile, your most impactful contributions, like preventing system failures or scaling team processes, might go completely unnoticed unless you surface them intentionally.

与此同时，你最有影响力的贡献——比如防止系统故障、或扩展团队流程——可能完全不被注意，除非你有意识地把它们呈现出来。

The simplest way to assess your progress as a tech lead is by measuring yourself against the goals you've set. These goals act as your compass; they help define what success looks like in the short term and give you something concrete to aim for.

评估你作为技术负责人进步的最简单方式，是用你自己设定的目标来衡量自己。这些目标像你的指南针；它们帮你定义短期内的成功长什么样，并给你一个具体可瞄准的东西。

Setting these goals should be part of your broader growth plan. You can read all about how to develop one in the section "Developing a Personal Growth Plan" on page 38.

设定这些目标，应该是你更宏大成长计划的一部分。你可以在第 38 页"制定个人成长计划"一节中读到如何制定它。

— PDF p.349 —

Set one or two focused goals each quarter based on what your team or organization needs most. For example:

每个季度根据你的团队或组织最需要什么，设定一两个聚焦的目标。比如：

  • Improve team visibility by launching a monthly showcase for stakeholders.通过为干系人发起每月一次的展示会，提升团队可见度。
  • Strengthen cross-team communication by setting up a recurring sync with adjacent product teams.通过与相邻产品团队建立定期同步，加强跨团队沟通。
  • Expand our impact by taking ownership of the internal authentication service and driving its roadmap.通过接管内部认证服务并驱动其路线图，扩大我们的影响力。

These goals should connect back to your team. After all, your success as a tech lead is inseparable from how well your team is doing. Set goals that reflect their growth, unblock their challenges, and support their performance. The clearest signal that you're on the right path? A thriving, confident, high-performing

这些目标应该与你的团队相连。毕竟，你作为技术负责人的成功，与团队做得怎么样密不可分。设定反映他们成长、为他们解除挑战、支持他们表现的目标。你走在正确道路上最清晰的信号是什么？那就是一支蓬勃、自信、高绩效的

— PDF p.350 —

team. These goals may feel outside your control at first, but that's part of stepping into leadership. The good news is: you have more influence than you think.

团队。这些目标一开始可能感觉超出你的控制，但这正是走上领导力之路的一部分。好消息是：你拥有的影响力比你以为的更大。

Revisit these goals regularly. Ask yourself: Have I made visible progress? Have I unblocked or accelerated anything as a result? What feedback have I received that supports or challenges this progress?

定期复盘这些目标。问自己：我取得了可见的进展吗？我因此为某些事解除了阻塞或加速了它吗？我收到了哪些支持或挑战这一进展的反馈？

Anchoring your growth to these clearly defined goals not only helps you reflect and course-correct along the way; it also gives you a practical, proactive way to demonstrate your value as a tech lead: with measurable progress rather than abstract qualities.

把你的成长锚定在这些明确定义的目标上，不仅帮你一路反思和纠偏；还给你一种实用、主动的方式来证明你作为技术负责人的价值：用可衡量的进展，而不是抽象的品质。

Another useful way to assess your impact as a leader is to pay attention to your gut feeling. Are you consistently hearing positive feedback, or are there recurring concerns about certain aspects of your leadership? Do people come to you for guidance and decision making? If not, what might be preventing that? These are powerful indicators of how you're perceived and whether your leadership is being felt.

另一个评估你作为领导者影响力的有用方式，是关注你的直觉。你是否持续听到正面反馈？还是在你领导力的某些方面反复出现顾虑？人们会来找你寻求指引和做决策吗？如果不，是什么在阻碍？这些都是关于你如何被看待、以及你的领导是否被感受到的强力指标。

Your gut instinct can offer valuable signals, but it's just one input. To validate it, you need to seek out direct feedback. To get a more complete picture, gather feedback from all directions, for both yourself and your team. This means team members, stakeholders, partner teams, cross-functional collaborators, even clients or users.

你的直觉可以提供有价值的信号，但它只是一个输入。要验证它，你需要主动寻求直接反馈。要得到更完整的画面，从所有方向收集反馈——既为你自己，也为你的团队。这意味着团队成员、干系人、伙伴团队、跨职能协作者，甚至客户或用户。

You can start small. Sometimes all it takes is a casual check-in: "Hey, I've been thinking about how we've been working together lately. Is there anything I could do to make collaboration easier?"

你可以从小处开始。有时候，一次随意的寒暄就够了："嘿，我最近一直在想我们最近一起工作的方式。有什么我能做的，让协作更顺畅吗？"
